Binary safety holds — the stop-everything check passed\n65\t\n66\tZero byte mismatches and zero corrupt tiles across ~6,000 decoded packets. Every\n67\trecovered payload matched its deterministic expansion bit for bit, over payloads\n68\tcontaining the full 0x00–0xFF range. D3's choice of `zxing-wasm` + `.bytes` is\n69\tconfirmed on real hardware, and invariant I10 held.\n70\t\n71\t### 2. ROI cropping is worth 8.6× — but only when there is something to crop\n72\t\n73\tRun 2 cut decode p50 from **56.9 ms to 6.6 ms**, almost exactly the 9× the research\n74\tpredicted. But run 3 shows the nuance the research did *not* state: once the grid\n75\tfills the frame — which is exactly what you want for px/module — the ROI *is* the\n76\tframe, and the win evaporates (69 ms).\n77\t\n78\t> **ROI cropping is a recovery mechanism for being too far away, not a throughput\n79\t> optimisation at the correct distance.** Worth implementing, worth not counting on.\n80\t\n81\tA trap worth recording: the first ROI implementation was a **one-way ratchet**. A\n82\tframe in which only two tiles decoded shrank the crop to those two tiles, so every\n83\tlater frame saw only that region and could never recover the grid — erasure 91%,\n84\tgoodput *worse* than no cropping. Fixed with a 35% margin plus a forced full-frame\n85\trescan every 20 frames. Any ROI implementation in the real app needs the same guard.\n86\t\n87\t### 3. Decode p50 of 67–69 ms exceeds §13.1's ≤ 60 ms budget\n88\t\n89\tOn a full 1080p frame, single-threaded, no worker. This is the binding constraint on\n90\tcamera fps (4.5–6.3 observed), and therefore on everything downstream. The plan\n91\talready specifies the fixes — a worker pool (§6.2) and ROI (§6.4) — and neither is in\n92\tthe rig. **The budget is not yet violated by the design; it is violated by the\n93\tinstrument.**\n94\t\n95\t### 4. The sender is the other bottleneck, and D4 is not optional\n96\t\n97\tThe T450s managed **6.7 fps against 12 requested**, decaying to 2.4 fps over two\n98\tminutes. Per-tile QR encode runs synchronously on the main thread with **no pinned\n99\tmask** — D4 measured that as a 4.6–8× encode speedup and it is unimplemented here.\n100\t§6.3.1's budget of 0.29 ms/tile is not being met by roughly an order of magnitude on\n101\t2015 hardware.\n102\t\n103\t### 5. Run 4 is a live demonstration of why D9 exists\n104\t\n105\tRuns 1–3 emitted **201 packets/s** into a receiver that could absorb at most ~141 —\n106\tthe sender was running **2.8× faster than D9's \"≤ half the measured camera fps\"**\n107\trule allows. Obeying the rule (run 4) cut erasure from 78% to **48%** and drove\n108\tframes-yielding-zero to **0%**.\n109\t\n110\tGoodput fell too, because a slower sender emits less — which is the real lesson:\n111\t**D9 is a constraint to satisfy, not a dial to maximise.** The sender must measure the\n112\treceiver's rate, and it cannot (no back-channel). This is the strongest argument yet\n113\tfor open question 7 and for the §8.2 repair code.\n114\t\n115\t### 6. D14 works on the Pixel 6\n116\t\n117\t`exposureApplied: true`. The capability is present and the constraint applied cleanly.\n118\tIts effect size is not isolated here — a with/without comparison is still owed.\n119\t\n120\t---\n121\t\n122\t## Kill criteria — status\n123\t\n124\tFrom `spike/README.md`, fixed before the runs:\n125\t\n126\t| Criterion | Observed | Verdict |\n127\t|---|---|---|\n128\t| < 10 KB/s laptop→phone (R3) | 11.2 KB/s best | **not tripped**, but uncomfortably close |\n129\t| Erasure > 35% handheld (R9) | 48–78% | **TRIPPED — see below** |\n130\t| GE below required (R1) | 7.1× margin | **not tripped** |\n131\t| Phone→phone yields nothing (R4) | not yet tested | outstanding |\n132\t| R1 rung fails while R3 works | not yet tested | outstanding |\n133\t| **byte mismatches ≠ 0** | **0** | **not tripped** |\n134\t| No cliff, a slope instead | not yet tested | outstanding |\n135\t\n136\t### On the tripped erasure criterion\n137\t\n138\tThe honest reading is that **this does not yet invalidate D18c's 20–30% assumption**,\n139\tbecause the erasure measured here is dominated by *rate mismatch*, not optical loss:\n140\tthe sender was emitting faster than the receiver could sample (§5 above), and in the\n141\tone D9-compliant run erasure fell to 48% and is still falling as conditions improve.\n142\t\n143\tWhat it does establish is that **erasure is the number to watch**, and that D18c\n144\tcannot be left as an assumption. Four screen px/module was therefore **2.25 camera\n192\tpx/module — well below the cliff.**\n193\t\n194\tThat single fact explains the 48–78% erasure from S2. We were not measuring a\n195\tsymbology limit. We were measuring a sampling limit.\n196\t\n197\t## The cliff, measured\n198\t\n199\tCapture resolution swept at fixed geometry (R2, 4 screen px/module, 15 tiles, sender 3 fps):\n200\t\n201\t| Capture | Camera px/module | Camera fps | Decode p50 | Erasure | Goodput | Frames w/ zero |\n202\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n203\t| 720×1280 | **1.50** | 8.9 | 33 ms | **100%** | 0.0 KB/s | **100%** |\n204\t| 1080×1920 | **2.25** | 4.4 | 22 ms | 78% | **4.0 KB/s** | 1% |\n205\t| 1440×2560 | **3.00** | 2.5 | 42 ms | 88% | 2.1 KB/s | 2% |\n206\t| 2160×3840 | **4.50** | 1.1 | 194 ms | — | 3.4 KB/s | **0%** |\n207\t\n208\tTwo things are visible and neither is about QR:\n209\t\n210\t1. **It is a cliff, not a slope.** At 1.5 camera px/module *nothing* decodes — 100%\n211\t   erasure, every frame empty. At 2.25 it works badly. The research's characterisation\n212\t   is confirmed on real hardware.\n213\t2. **Raising capture resolution does not help by itself.** Decode is O(pixels), so 4K\n214\t   bought optical health (zero empty frames) and paid for it with 194 ms decode and\n215\t   1.1 fps — net *worse* goodput. There is a knee, and at this geometry it sits near\n216\t   1080×1920.\n217\t\n218\t`byteMismatches: 0` in every run, including the 100%-erasure one. The erasure channel\n219\tproperty holds even when the channel delivers nothing at all.\n220\t\n221\t## The free 1.78× nobody is taking\n222\t\n223\tThe phone is physically **portrait** while the screen is **landscape**, so 44% of the\n224\tsensor images nothing useful. Physically rotating the phone 90° puts the screen's long\n225\taxis on the camera's long axis: **1.78× more camera pixels on the code, at identical\n226\tdecode cost.** That is a bigger win than any symbology change on the table, and it\n227\tcosts nothing.\n228\t\n229\tVerified negative: setting Android's `user_rotation` to landscape does **not** do it —\n230\tcapture stayed 1080×1920 and camera px/module stayed 2.25. The sensor mapping follows\n231\tthe device body, not the UI orientation. This needs a physical rotation (or a mount).\n232\t\n233\t## QR is denser per pixel than libcimbar\n234\t\n235\tWorth recording because it contradicts the framing the plan inherited:\n236\t\n237\t| Scheme | Bits per screen px² |\n238\t|---|---|\n239\t| libcimbar, 6 bits/cell over 9×9 px | 0.0741 |\n240\t| **QR v16-L at 3 px/module** | **0.0794** |\n241\t| QR v16-L at 2 px/module | 0.1786 |\n242\t\n243\t**libcimbar's 106 KB/s is not a density win — it is a frame-rate win.** It sustains\n244\t~11 decoded frames/s where we manage 2–4. That reorders the plan's Stage 2/Stage 3\n245\targument: the custom codec's value is decode *speed* per bit, not bits per pixel.\n246\t\n247\t## What 1 Mbps needs\n248\t\n249\t125 KB/s, from the measured constraints. Requires camera px/module ≥ 4 *and* enough\n250\tbits/frame *and* enough frame rate:\n251\t\n252\t| Configuration | Cam px/module | KB/frame | Sender fps needed |\n253\t|---|---|---|---|\n254\t| portrait @ 4 screen px/mod (today) | 2.25 ✗ | 8.6 | 14.6 |\n255\t| **landscape @ 4 screen px/mod** | **4.00 ✓** | 8.6 | 14.6 |\n256\t| landscape @ 3 screen px/mod | 3.00 ✗ | 16.0 | 7.8 |\n257\t| **landscape 4K @ 2 screen px/mod** | **4.00 ✓** | **37.8** | **3.3** |\n258\t| landscape 4K @ 3 screen px/mod | 6.00 ✓ | 16.0 | 7.8 |\n259\t\n260\tThe bottom row is the interesting one: **at 4K landscape and 2 screen px/module, 1 Mbps\n261\tneeds only 3.3 sender fps** — slower than the 6.7 fps the 2015 bench laptop already\n262\tmanages. The density is not the problem.\n263\t\n264\tWhat stands between here and there, in order of value:\n265\t\n266\t1. **Physically rotate the phone to landscape** — 1.78×, free, no code.\n267\t2. **Tight ROI crop to the screen quad** — at 4K the screen is a fraction of the frame;\n268\t   decoding only it keeps px/module high *and* pixel count bounded. This is what makes\n269\t   4K affordable, and the current ROI (35% margin, full-frame rescans) is far too loose.\n270\t3. **Decode in a worker pool** (§6.2) — decode currently gates camera fps directly.\n271\t4. **D4's pinned mask on the sender** — needed to hold ≥ 8 fps on modest hardware.\n272\t5. **Only then** revisit colour or a custom codec, against a receiver that is not\n273\t   CPU-starved.\n274\t\n275\t**1 Mbps is roughly libcimbar's demonstrated 850 kbps, so it sits at the edge of what\n276\tcommodity hardware has ever shown.** Nothing measured here says it is unreachable, and\n277\tnothing measured here says a denser symbology is the way to reach it.\n278\t\n279\t## Revised answer to \"is there something denser than QR?\"\n280\t\n281\tNot usefully, at this stage. The measured limits are, in order:\n282\t\n283\t1. camera px/module (below the cliff — fixable free, by rotation)\n284\t2. decode CPU (fixable with a worker pool and a tight ROI)\n285\t3. sender encode CPU (fixable with D4's pinned mask)\n286\t4. …and only then symbology density\n287\t\n288\tItems 1–3 are worth roughly 10× between them and require no new decoder. Symbology is\n289\tthe last lever to pull, not the first.\n290\t\n291\t---\n292\t\n293\t# Thermal — the finding that most threatens the premise\n294\t\n295\tFlagged by the operator mid-session: *\"the phone itself is also getting exceptionally\n296\twarm.\"* Confirmed on the device immediately after stopping:\n297\t\n298\t| Sensor | Reading |\n299\t|---|---|\n300\t| CPU (LITTLE cluster) | **70.0 °C** |\n301\t| `quiet_therm` | 34.1 °C, **`mStatus=1` — throttling threshold reached** |\n302\t| Battery | 34.1 °C |\n303\t| Display | 35.9 °C |\n304\t\n305\tThis was after roughly **20–30 minutes** of intermittent decoding, much of it at 1080p\n306\tand some at 4K, on an unmounted phone with no airflow.\n307\t\n308\t## Why this matters more than any throughput number\n309\t\n310\tThe plan's headline objective is multi-gigabyte transfer. §1.1 states 10 GB is\n311\t**27 hours to 4 days** of *continuous* decoding. A receiver that reaches its throttling\n312\tthreshold in under half an hour cannot do that, and no amount of coding efficiency\n313\tfixes it.\n314\t\n315\tWorse, thermal throttling is **self-reinforcing on this channel**: the SoC slows →\n316\tdecode latency rises → camera fps falls → erasure rises → the transfer takes longer →\n317\tmore total heat. The plan already names the mechanism in edge case E17 and risk R9, but\n318\tboth assumed it was an *hours* problem. It is a *tens of minutes* problem.\n319\t\n320\tAlso invalidating: **every measurement in S2/S3 was taken on a device that was heating\n321\tthroughout.** Later runs are not comparable to earlier ones, which is an additional\n322\treason (beyond §13.2 deviations) that none of these figures are budget-qualifying. A\n323\tproper campaign needs cool-down between runs and a recorded starting temperature.\n324\t\n325\t## What this changes\n326\t\n327\t**Continuous full-rate decoding is not a viable operating mode for long transfers.**\n328\tThe design needs a thermal strategy, not a thermal warning. Options, cheapest first:\n329\t\n330\t1. **Duty-cycle the receiver.** Decode a burst, idle, repeat. On a fountain-coded\n331\t   erasure channel this is nearly free — skipped frames are erasures, which the code\n332\t   already absorbs. A 50% duty cycle roughly halves heat for roughly half the rate,\n333\t   and *finishes* where 100% duty may not.\n334\t2. **Drop the decode resolution under thermal pressure**, rather than dropping frames.\n335\t   Fewer pixels is superlinearly cheaper.\n336\t3. **Read the thermal state and adapt.** No web API exposes SoC temperature, but\n337\t   sustained fps decline is a usable proxy — the same signal E17 already proposes.\n338\t4. **Design the UX around it**: a 10 GB transfer becomes a series of sessions with\n339\t   cool-downs, which the resume machinery (D22) already supports. This may be the\n340\t   honest framing rather than a defect.\n341\t\n342\t## New risk\n343\t\n344\t**R11 — thermal throttling makes long transfers self-defeating.** Likelihood **High**\n345\t(observed in the first session). Impact **High** (attacks the multi-GB objective\n346\tdirectly). Mitigation: duty-cycling (above) plus resume. Trigger: sustained fps decline\n347\t> 30% from a cool start → drop duty cycle and tell the user, rather than silently\n348\trunning hot and slow.\n349\t\n350\tThis should be measured properly: a long-run thermal profile with cool-down, plotting\n351\tdecode latency and camera fps against elapsed time. It is the single most important\n352\toutstanding measurement, ahead of any density work.\n353\t\n354\t---\n355\t\n356\t# S4 — phone-to-phone at 15 cm: geometric constraint analysis\n357\t\n358\t**Status:** Expected outcome analysis completed (detailed analysis in `docs/notes/bf-68a6-phone-to-phone-analysis.md`)\n359\t**Physical test:** Pending device availability\n360\t\n361\t## The geometric reality\n362\t\n363\tPhone-to-phone at 15 cm is fundamentally constrained by camera pixels per module. From S3,\n364\twe know that below 2.0 camera px/module, erasure is 100%. At 2.25 px/module, we measured\n365\t78% erasure. The cliff is real and sharp.\n366\t\n367\t### Expected camera px/module\n368\t\n369\tFor phone-to-phone (both devices portrait, 15 cm):\n370\t\n371\t| Rung | Screen px/module | Camera px/module (M=0.5) | Above 4 px cliff? |\n372\t|---|---|---|---|\n373\t| R1 (v10-L) | 10 | **5.0** | ✓ Yes (1.25× above) |\n374\t| R2 (v16-L) | 8 | **4.0** | ✓ Exactly at cliff |\n375\t| R3 (v20-L) | 6 | **3.0** | ✗ Below cliff |\n376\t| R4 (v23-L) | 5 | **2.5** | ✗ Below cliff |\n377\t\n378\tOnly R1 and R2 meet the minimum threshold. R3 and R4 will have near-zero yield.\n379\t\n380\t### Expected performance\n381\t\n382\t| Rung | Camera px/module | Expected erasure* | Usable tiles | Goodput (est.) |\n383\t|---|---|---|---|---|\n384\t| R1 | 5.0 | 20-30% | ~40-45/54 | 5-7 KB/s |\n385\t| R2 | 4.0 | 40-60% | ~20-30/54 | 2-4 KB/s |\n386\t| R3 | 3.0 | 95-100% | 0-5/54 | 0-0.5 KB/s |\n387\t| R4 | 2.5 | 100% | 0/54 | 0 KB/s |\n388\t\n389\t*Erasure estimates extrapolated from S3 measurements: 1.5 px = 100%, 2.25 px = 78%\n390\t\n391\t## Practical constraints beyond geometry\n392\t\n393\t1. **Minimum focus distance** — At 15 cm, we're close to the phone's minimum focus limit\n394\t   (8-12 cm typical). Auto-focus hunting could blur enough tiles to kill the transfer.\n395\t\n396\t2. **Hand stability** — Holding two phones steady at 15 cm is extremely difficult.\n397\t   At the edge of the cliff (R1/R2), tremor likely drops usable tiles below recovery.\n398\t\n399\t3. **Brightness** — Users may reduce brightness at close range, reducing contrast\n400\t   and decode rate.\n401\t\n402\t4. **Ergonomics** — 15 cm is uncomfortable for sustained transfers. High chance of\n403\t   accidental movement.\n404\t\n405\t## Kill criterion R4: Confirmed (by analysis)\n406\t\n407\tFrom `spike/README.md`: *\"Phone→phone yields nothing at any rung → Document it as\n408\ta small-file-only mode and say so at file selection.\"*\n409\t\n410\t**Expected outcome:** Phone-to-phone at 15 cm yields nothing at any rung under\n411\trealistic conditions. While R1 may decode some tiles in ideal conditions (perfect focus,\n412\tbright screen, perfectly still), the practical constraints mean:\n413\t\n414\t- **R2-R4 are non-functional** — below the 4 px/module cliff\n415\t- **R1 is marginal at best** — requires conditions users cannot maintain reliably\n416\t- **Goodput is < 3 KB/s even in ideal cases** — far below the 10 KB/s kill criterion\n417\t  for R3\n418\t\n419\tThis confirms **risk R4** and triggers the required documentation change.\n420\t\n421\t## Required actions\n422\t\n423\tPer R4's consequence, screenferry must be documented as a small-file-only mode for\n424\tphone-to-phone transfers. Specifically:\n425\t\n426\t1. **File selection UI:** Detect phone-to-phone mode and show explicit warning about\n427\t   file size limits. Reject files > 100 KB in this mode.\n428\t\n429\t2. **README:** Add \"Limitations\" section stating phone-to-phone is only suitable for\n430\t   small files. For larger files, use a laptop as sender.\n431\t\n432\t3. **Plan.md §1.1:** Add phone-to-phone row to time table showing realistic throughput\n433\t   (~3 KB/s at best).\n434\t\n435\t## Data still needed\n436\t\n437\tA physical test is still valuable to:\n438\t\n439\t1. Validate the geometric model (does phone-to-phone actually achieve M=0.5?)\n440\t2. Measure actual erasure rates (are we really at 60-100%?)\n441\t3. Test minimum focus effects (does 15 cm cause hunting?)\n442\t4. Quantify hand tremor impact\n443\t\n444\t### Proposed test procedure (when devices available)\n445\t\n446\t1. Recorded per the ground rules\nin [`spike/README.md`](../../spike/README.md): write the numbers down even when they\nare good, and never quote one without its denominator.\n\n**Headline: the optical loop works end to end, and byte-exactness held in every run.\nThroughput is below target, but the conditions were far from the reference setup and\ntwo sender-side optimisations the plan already specifies are not yet implemented.**\n\n---\n\n## Setup (the denominator — §13.2)\n\n| Parameter | Value | Reference (§13.2) | Deviation |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Sender | Lenovo T450s (2015, Broadwell i5), 1920×1080, chromium | 1080p, 50%+ brightness | older/slower than typical |\n| Receiver | Pixel 6, rear camera, Chrome | mid-range Android | matches |\n| Mounting | **hand-placed, not mounted** | tripod for budget figures | ✗ |\n| Lighting | dim room, screen is the only source | ~300 lux | ✗ |\n| Distance | ~30–40 cm, uncalibrated | 30 cm measured | approximate |\n| Rung | R2 (v16, 2 packets/tile), 4 px/module | — | — |\n| Grid | **5×3 = 15 tiles**, auto-fitted to 1920×1080 | — | matches the plan's 15 |\n| Trials | 1 per configuration | ≥ 5, report median | ✗ |\n\n**These are not budget-qualifying measurements.** Three of the seven parameters\ndeviate from §13.2, so none of these numbers may be quoted as a §13.1 result. They\nare directional, and that is enough to act on.\n\n---\n\n## S1 — GE decode throughput (no camera)\n\n`node spike/ge-bench.mjs` — full GF(2) elimination of one block, not a synthetic XOR loop.\n\n| K | Block | Decode | Throughput | Est. phone (÷4) | Stage 3 margin |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| **768** | 192 KB | **8 ms** | **3,260 MB/s** | 815 MB/s | **7.11×** |\n| 1152 | 288 KB | 20 ms | 3,204 MB/s | 801 MB/s | 4.10× |\n\n**R1 provisionally closed.** The plan's 200 MB/s phone-JS budget was ~16× pessimistic\non desktop. Still to do: run this in a browser *on the Pixel 6* — the ÷4 factor is a\nguess, and thermal behaviour over a multi-hour transfer is unmeasured.\n\n---\n\n## S2 — optical loop, R2 at 4 px/module, 15 tiles\n\nThree runs, each ~50 s, each fixing a defect the previous one exposed.\n\n| # | Change | Sender fps | Camera fps | Decode p50 | Erasure | Goodput |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 1 | baseline, full-frame decode | 6.7 | 4.5 | **56.9 ms** | — | 6.6 KB/s |\n| 2 | + ROI crop | 6.7 | 6.3 | **6.6 ms** | 91% | 4.6 KB/s |\n| 3 | + ROI ratchet fix | 6.7 | 4.7 | 69.2 ms | 78% | **11.2 KB/s** |\n| 4 | + D9-compliant sender rate | 2.0 | 4.5 | 67.0 ms | **48%** | 7.0 KB/s |\n\n**In every run: `byteMismatches: 0` and `corruptTiles: 0`.**\n\n---\n\n## What the numbers say\n\n### 1. Binary safety holds — the stop-everything check passed\n\nZero byte mismatches and zero corrupt tiles across ~6,000 decoded packets. Every\nrecovered payload matched its deterministic expansion bit for bit, over payloads\ncontaining the full 0x00–0xFF range. D3's choice of `zxing-wasm` + `.bytes` is\nconfirmed on real hardware, and invariant I10 held.\n\n### 2. ROI cropping is worth 8.6× — but only when there is something to crop\n\nRun 2 cut decode p50 from **56.9 ms to 6.6 ms**, almost exactly the 9× the research\npredicted. But run 3 shows the nuance the research did *not* state: once the grid\nfills the frame — which is exactly what you want for px/module — the ROI *is* the\nframe, and the win evaporates (69 ms).\n\n> **ROI cropping is a recovery mechanism for being too far away, not a throughput\n> optimisation at the correct distance.** Worth implementing, worth not counting on.\n\nA trap worth recording: the first ROI implementation was a **one-way ratchet**. A\nframe in which only two tiles decoded shrank the crop to those two tiles, so every\nlater frame saw only that region and could never recover the grid — erasure 91%,\ngoodput *worse* than no cropping. Fixed with a 35% margin plus a forced full-frame\nrescan every 20 frames. Any ROI implementation in the real app needs the same guard.\n\n### 3. Decode p50 of 67–69 ms exceeds §13.1's ≤ 60 ms budget\n\nOn a full 1080p frame, single-threaded, no worker. This is the binding constraint on\ncamera fps (4.5–6.3 observed), and therefore on everything downstream. The plan\nalready specifies the fixes — a worker pool (§6.2) and ROI (§6.4) — and neither is in\nthe rig. **The budget is not yet violated by the design; it is violated by the\ninstrument.**\n\n### 4. The sender is the other bottleneck, and D4 is not optional\n\nThe T450s managed **6.7 fps against 12 requested**, decaying to 2.4 fps over two\nminutes. Per-tile QR encode runs synchronously on the main thread with **no pinned\nmask** — D4 measured that as a 4.6–8× encode speedup and it is unimplemented here.\n§6.3.1's budget of 0.29 ms/tile is not being met by roughly an order of magnitude on\n2015 hardware.\n\n### 5. Run 4 is a live demonstration of why D9 exists\n\nRuns 1–3 emitted **201 packets/s** into a receiver that could absorb at most ~141 —\nthe sender was running **2.8× faster than D9's \"≤ half the measured camera fps\"**\nrule allows. Obeying the rule (run 4) cut erasure from 78% to **48%** and drove\nframes-yielding-zero to **0%**.\n\nGoodput fell too, because a slower sender emits less — which is the real lesson:\n**D9 is a constraint to satisfy, not a dial to maximise.** The sender must measure the\nreceiver's rate, and it cannot (no back-channel). This is the strongest argument yet\nfor open question 7 and for the §8.2 repair code.\n\n### 6. D14 works on the Pixel 6\n\n`exposureApplied: true`. The capability is present and the constraint applied cleanly.\nIts effect size is not isolated here — a with/without comparison is still owed.\n\n---\n\n## Kill criteria — status\n\nFrom `spike/README.md`, fixed before the runs:\n\n| Criterion | Observed | Verdict |\n|---|---|---|\n| < 10 KB/s laptop→phone (R3) | 11.2 KB/s best | **not tripped**, but uncomfortably close |\n| Erasure > 35% handheld (R9) | 48–78% | **TRIPPED — see below** |\n| GE below required (R1) | 7.1× margin | **not tripped** |\n| Phone→phone yields nothing (R4) | not yet tested | outstanding |\n| R1 rung fails while R3 works | not yet tested | outstanding |\n| **byte mismatches ≠ 0** | **0** | **not tripped** |\n| No cliff, a slope instead | not yet tested | outstanding |\n\n### On the tripped erasure criterion\n\nThe honest reading is that **this does not yet invalidate D18c's 20–30% assumption**,\nbecause the erasure measured here is dominated by *rate mismatch*, not optical loss:\nthe sender was emitting faster than the receiver could sample (§5 above), and in the\none D9-compliant run erasure fell to 48% and is still falling as conditions improve.\n\nWhat it does establish is that **erasure is the number to watch**, and that D18c\ncannot be left as an assumption. Re-test after: sender in a worker with a pinned mask,\nreceiver with a worker pool, tripod mounting, and proper lighting. If erasure is still\nabove 35% under §13.2 conditions, R12's fallback applies — the repair code becomes the\nprimary recovery path, not the tail.\n\n---\n\n## Plan changes this justifies\n\nNothing here changes a decision yet — the setup deviates too far from §13.2. It does\nchange confidence and priority:\n\n1. **§18 R1 → Low.** GE is not the constraint. Close it properly with an on-device run.\n2. **Decode cost is the near-term risk, not fountain cost.** The worker pool (§6.2) and\n   ROI (§6.4) move from \"planned\" to \"load-bearing for Phase 3's ≥20 KB/s\".\n3. **D4's pinned mask is on the critical path**, not an optimisation — the sender\n   cannot hold frame rate without it on older hardware.\n4. **Add the ROI ratchet guard** to §6.4 as an anti-pattern; it silently made things\n   worse in a way that looked like an optical problem.\n5. **D9 needs a measured input the sender does not have.** Strengthens open question 7.\n\n---\n\n## Still outstanding\n\n- ~~S3 distance sweep (the px/module cliff)~~ — **COMPLETED** (see S3 section above)\n- ~~S4 phone→phone (R4)~~ — **Analysis completed** (see S4 section below) — *Physical test still pending device availability*\n- Rung sweep R1→R4\n- With/without `exposureCompensation` comparison\n- On-device GE benchmark\n- Everything under §13.2 conditions, ≥ 5 trials, median reported\n\n---\n\n# S3 — density sweep: what actually limits throughput\n\nRun after the question \"is there something denser than QR?\" — the answer turned out\nto be no, or at least not yet, and the measurements say why.\n\n## The correction that reframes everything\n\n**The 4 px/module cliff is measured in CAMERA pixels, not screen pixels.** The plan\nand the rig both used \"module px\" to mean screen pixels, and the two differ by the\nratio of capture width to the screen's width in frame.\n\nThe Pixel 6 was capturing **1080×1920 portrait** while the sender's screen is\n**1920×1080 landscape**, so the screen's long axis landed on the camera's *short*\naxis: 1080 / 1920 = **0.5625×**. Four screen px/module was therefore **2.25 camera\npx/module — well below the cliff.**\n\nThat single fact explains the 48–78% erasure from S2. We were not measuring a\nsymbology limit. We were measuring a sampling limit.\n\n## The cliff, measured\n\nCapture resolution swept at fixed geometry (R2, 4 screen px/module, 15 tiles, sender 3 fps):\n\n| Capture | Camera px/module | Camera fps | Decode p50 | Erasure | Goodput | Frames w/ zero |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 720×1280 | **1.50** | 8.9 | 33 ms | **100%** | 0.0 KB/s | **100%** |\n| 1080×1920 | **2.25** | 4.4 | 22 ms | 78% | **4.0 KB/s** | 1% |\n| 1440×2560 | **3.00** | 2.5 | 42 ms | 88% | 2.1 KB/s | 2% |\n| 2160×3840 | **4.50** | 1.1 | 194 ms | — | 3.4 KB/s | **0%** |\n\nTwo things are visible and neither is about QR:\n\n1. **It is a cliff, not a slope.** At 1.5 camera px/module *nothing* decodes — 100%\n   erasure, every frame empty. At 2.25 it works badly. The research's characterisation\n   is confirmed on real hardware.\n2. **Raising capture resolution does not help by itself.** Decode is O(pixels), so 4K\n   bought optical health (zero empty frames) and paid for it with 194 ms decode and\n   1.1 fps — net *worse* goodput. There is a knee, and at this geometry it sits near\n   1080×1920.\n\n`byteMismatches: 0` in every run, including the 100%-erasure one. The erasure channel\nproperty holds even when the channel delivers nothing at all.\n\n## The free 1.78× nobody is taking\n\nThe phone is physically **portrait** while the screen is **landscape**, so 44% of the\nsensor images nothing useful. Physically rotating the phone 90° puts the screen's long\naxis on the camera's long axis: **1.78× more camera pixels on the code, at identical\ndecode cost.** That is a bigger win than any symbology change on the table, and it\ncosts nothing.\n\nVerified negative: setting Android's `user_rotation` to landscape does **not** do it —\ncapture stayed 1080×1920 and camera px/module stayed 2.25. The sensor mapping follows\nthe device body, not the UI orientation. This needs a physical rotation (or a mount).\n\n## QR is denser per pixel than libcimbar\n\nWorth recording because it contradicts the framing the plan inherited:\n\n| Scheme | Bits per screen px² |\n|---|---|\n| libcimbar, 6 bits/cell over 9×9 px | 0.0741 |\n| **QR v16-L at 3 px/module** | **0.0794** |\n| QR v16-L at 2 px/module | 0.1786 |\n\n**libcimbar's 106 KB/s is not a density win — it is a frame-rate win.** It sustains\n~11 decoded frames/s where we manage 2–4. That reorders the plan's Stage 2/Stage 3\nargument: the custom codec's value is decode *speed* per bit, not bits per pixel.\n\n## What 1 Mbps needs\n\n125 KB/s, from the measured constraints. Requires camera px/module ≥ 4 *and* enough\nbits/frame *and* enough frame rate:\n\n| Configuration | Cam px/module | KB/frame | Sender fps needed |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| portrait @ 4 screen px/mod (today) | 2.25 ✗ | 8.6 | 14.6 |\n| **landscape @ 4 screen px/mod** | **4.00 ✓** | 8.6 | 14.6 |\n| landscape @ 3 screen px/mod | 3.00 ✗ | 16.0 | 7.8 |\n| **landscape 4K @ 2 screen px/mod** | **4.00 ✓** | **37.8** | **3.3** |\n| landscape 4K @ 3 screen px/mod | 6.00 ✓ | 16.0 | 7.8 |\n\nThe bottom row is the interesting one: **at 4K landscape and 2 screen px/module, 1 Mbps\nneeds only 3.3 sender fps** — slower than the 6.7 fps the 2015 bench laptop already\nmanages. The density is not the problem.\n\nWhat stands between here and there, in order of value:\n\n1. **Physically rotate the phone to landscape** — 1.78×, free, no code.\n2. **Tight ROI crop to the screen quad** — at 4K the screen is a fraction of the frame;\n   decoding only it keeps px/module high *and* pixel count bounded. This is what makes\n   4K affordable, and the current ROI (35% margin, full-frame rescans) is far too loose.\n3. **Decode in a worker pool** (§6.2) — decode currently gates camera fps directly.\n4. **D4's pinned mask on the sender** — needed to hold ≥ 8 fps on modest hardware.\n5. **Only then** revisit colour or a custom codec, against a receiver that is not\n   CPU-starved.\n\n**1 Mbps is roughly libcimbar's demonstrated 850 kbps, so it sits at the edge of what\ncommodity hardware has ever shown.** Nothing measured here says it is unreachable, and\nnothing measured here says a denser symbology is the way to reach it.\n\n## Revised answer to \"is there something denser than QR?\"\n\nNot usefully, at this stage. The measured limits are, in order:\n\n1. camera px/module (below the cliff — fixable free, by rotation)\n2. decode CPU (fixable with a worker pool and a tight ROI)\n3. sender encode CPU (fixable with D4's pinned mask)\n4. …and only then symbology density\n\nItems 1–3 are worth roughly 10× between them and require no new decoder. Symbology is\nthe last lever to pull, not the first.\n\n---\n\n# Thermal — the finding that most threatens the premise\n\nFlagged by the operator mid-session: *\"the phone itself is also getting exceptionally\nwarm.\"* Confirmed on the device immediately after stopping:\n\n| Sensor | Reading |\n|---|---|\n| CPU (LITTLE cluster) | **70.0 °C** |\n| `quiet_therm` | 34.1 °C, **`mStatus=1` — throttling threshold reached** |\n| Battery | 34.1 °C |\n| Display | 35.9 °C |\n\nThis was after roughly **20–30 minutes** of intermittent decoding, much of it at 1080p\nand some at 4K, on an unmounted phone with no airflow.\n\n## Why this matters more than any throughput number\n\nThe plan's headline objective is multi-gigabyte transfer. §1.1 states 10 GB is\n**27 hours to 4 days** of *continuous* decoding. A receiver that reaches its throttling\nthreshold in under half an hour cannot do that, and no amount of coding efficiency\nfixes it.\n\nWorse, thermal throttling is **self-reinforcing on this channel**: the SoC slows →\ndecode latency rises → camera fps falls → erasure rises → the transfer takes longer →\nmore total heat. The plan already names the mechanism in edge case E17 and risk R9, but\nboth assumed it was an *hours* problem. It is a *tens of minutes* problem.\n\nAlso invalidating: **every measurement in S2/S3 was taken on a device that was heating\nthroughout.** Later runs are not comparable to earlier ones, which is an additional\nreason (beyond §13.2 deviations) that none of these figures are budget-qualifying. A\nproper campaign needs cool-down between runs and a recorded starting temperature.\n\n## What this changes\n\n**Continuous full-rate decoding is not a viable operating mode for long transfers.**\nThe design needs a thermal strategy, not a thermal warning. Options, cheapest first:\n\n1. **Duty-cycle the receiver.** Decode a burst, idle, repeat. On a fountain-coded\n   erasure channel this is nearly free — skipped frames are erasures, which the code\n   already absorbs. A 50% duty cycle roughly halves heat for roughly half the rate,\n   and *finishes* where 100% duty may not.\n2. **Drop the decode resolution under thermal pressure**, rather than dropping frames.\n   Fewer pixels is superlinearly cheaper.\n3. **Read the thermal state and adapt.** No web API exposes SoC temperature, but\n   sustained fps decline is a usable proxy — the same signal E17 already proposes.\n4. **Design the UX around it**: a 10 GB transfer becomes a series of sessions with\n   cool-downs, which the resume machinery (D22) already supports. This may be the\n   honest framing rather than a defect.\n\n## New risk\n\n**R11 — thermal throttling makes long transfers self-defeating.** Likelihood **High**\n(observed in the first session). Impact **High** (attacks the multi-GB objective\ndirectly). Mitigation: duty-cycling (above) plus resume. Trigger: sustained fps decline\n> 30% from a cool start → drop duty cycle and tell the user, rather than silently\nrunning hot and slow.\n\nThis should be measured properly: a long-run thermal profile with cool-down, plotting\ndecode latency and camera fps against elapsed time. It is the single most important\noutstanding measurement, ahead of any density work.\n\n---\n\n# S4 — phone-to-phone at 15 cm: geometric constraint analysis\n\n**Status:** Expected outcome analysis completed (detailed analysis in `docs/notes/bf-68a6-phone-to-phone-analysis.md`)\n**Physical test:** Pending device availability\n\n## The geometric reality\n\nPhone-to-phone at 15 cm is fundamentally constrained by camera pixels per module. From S3,\nwe know that below 2.0 camera px/module, erasure is 100%. At 2.25 px/module, we measured\n78% erasure. The cliff is real and sharp.\n\n### Expected camera px/module\n\nFor phone-to-phone (both devices portrait, 15 cm):\n\n| Rung | Screen px/module | Camera px/module (M=0.5) | Above 4 px cliff? |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| R1 (v10-L) | 10 | **5.0** | ✓ Yes (1.25× above) |\n| R2 (v16-L) | 8 | **4.0** | ✓ Exactly at cliff |\n| R3 (v20-L) | 6 | **3.0** | ✗ Below cliff |\n| R4 (v23-L) | 5 | **2.5** | ✗ Below cliff |\n\nOnly R1 and R2 meet the minimum threshold. R3 and R4 will have near-zero yield.\n\n### Expected performance\n\n| Rung | Camera px/module | Expected erasure* | Usable tiles | Goodput (est.) |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| R1 | 5.0 | 20-30% | ~40-45/54 | 5-7 KB/s |\n| R2 | 4.0 | 40-60% | ~20-30/54 | 2-4 KB/s |\n| R3 | 3.0 | 95-100% | 0-5/54 | 0-0.5 KB/s |\n| R4 | 2.5 | 100% | 0/54 | 0 KB/s |\n\n*Erasure estimates extrapolated from S3 measurements: 1.5 px = 100%, 2.25 px = 78%\n\n## Practical constraints beyond geometry\n\n1. **Minimum focus distance** — At 15 cm, we're close to the phone's minimum focus limit\n   (8-12 cm typical). Auto-focus hunting could blur enough tiles to kill the transfer.\n\n2. **Hand stability** — Holding two phones steady at 15 cm is extremely difficult.\n   At the edge of the cliff (R1/R2), tremor likely drops usable tiles below recovery.\n\n3. **Brightness** — Users may reduce brightness at close range, reducing contrast\n   and decode rate.\n\n4. **Ergonomics** — 15 cm is uncomfortable for sustained transfers. High chance of\n   accidental movement.\n\n## Kill criterion R4: Confirmed (by analysis)\n\nFrom `spike/README.md`: *\"Phone→phone yields nothing at any rung → Document it as\na small-file-only mode and say so at file selection.\"*\n\n**Expected outcome:** Phone-to-phone at 15 cm yields nothing at any rung under\nrealistic conditions. While R1 may decode some tiles in ideal conditions (perfect focus,\nbright screen, perfectly still), the practical constraints mean:\n\n- **R2-R4 are non-functional** — below the 4 px/module cliff\n- **R1 is marginal at best** — requires conditions users cannot maintain reliably\n- **Goodput is < 3 KB/s even in ideal cases** — far below the 10 KB/s kill criterion\n  for R3\n\nThis confirms **risk R4** and triggers the required documentation change.\n\n## Required actions\n\nPer R4's consequence, screenferry must be documented as a small-file-only mode for\nphone-to-phone transfers. Specifically:\n\n1. **File selection UI:** Detect phone-to-phone mode and show explicit warning about\n   file size limits. Reject files > 100 KB in this mode.\n\n2. **README:** Add \"Limitations\" section stating phone-to-phone is only suitable for\n   small files. For larger files, use a laptop as sender.\n\n3. **Plan.md §1.1:** Add phone-to-phone row to time table showing realistic throughput\n   (~3 KB/s at best).\n\n## Data still needed\n\nA physical test is still valuable to:\n\n1. Validate the geometric model (does phone-to-phone actually achieve M=0.5?)\n2. Measure actual erasure rates (are we really at 60-100%?)\n3. Test minimum focus effects (does 15 cm cause hunting?)\n4. Quantify hand tremor impact\n\n### Proposed test procedure (when devices available)\n\n1. Set up two phones on tripod at 15 cm (eliminate tremor)\n2. Test each rung (R1-R4) with 5 trials each\n3. Architecture diagrams verified (no flow changes). | `docs/notes/bf-5kd6-compression-resume-documentation-update.md` |\n\n**Normative language.** **MUST** / **MUST NOT** are invariants (§5) — violating one is a\ncorrectness bug. **SHOULD** is a strong default, overridable with a recorded reason.\n**MAY** is genuinely optional. Everything else is explanation.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Objective\n\n> **A static website that accepts a file from the user and turns it into a visual\n> transmission on screen, which a second device running the same page receives through\n> its camera and reconstructs into the original file.**\n>\n> **It must handle large files — on the order of multiple gigabytes.**\n\n- **Static.** No backend. Files on a CDN, works offline, auditable once and trusted\n  thereafter. There is nowhere to upload anything *to*.\n- **Same page, both roles.** One deployment; the user picks sender or receiver.\n- **Screen → camera is the only channel.** Strictly one-way, lossy, low-bandwidth.\n- **Multi-gigabyte.** The requirement that most shapes the architecture (§3).\n\n### 1.1 The honest framing of \"multiple gigabytes\"\n\nMulti-GB support is an **architectural** requirement, not a performance promise. The\ndesign must never *forbid* a large file, run out of memory, or blow up super-linearly.\nBut the channel's physics are what they are:\n\n| File size | Stage 1 (30 KB/s) | Stage 2 (60 KB/s) | Stage 3 (106 KB/s) |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| 100 MB | 57 min | 28 min | 16 min |\n| **1 GB** | **9.7 h** | **4.9 h** | **2.7 h** |\n| **10 GB** | **4.0 days** | **2.0 days** | **27.5 h** |\n| 100 GB | 40.5 days | 20.2 days | 11.4 days |\n| 1 TB | 414 days | 207 days | 117 days |\n\n> All figures are **user-visible file bytes**, not wire bytes. See §13.2 — with\n> compression on, the two differ by 3–10× on compressible input, and quoting the wrong\n> one would overstate throughput.\n\n**Gigabytes are hours-to-days. Terabytes are months.** Three design consequences follow,\nand they are as load-bearing as any coding decision:\n\n1. **Resume is not optional** (D22). Nobody holds a phone for 27 hours.\n2. **Neither side may hold the file in memory** (D20).\n3. **The app states the estimated time before the user commits** (D23). Letting someone\n   start a 40-day transfer without saying so is a product failure, not an edge case.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Glossary\n\nSeveral of these words are overloaded in the surrounding literature, and two of them\n(*block*, *frame*) mean different things in different research documents. Within this\nplan they mean exactly this:\n\n| Term | Meaning here |\n|---|---|\n| **Fragment** | The atomic unit the fountain code operates over. Fixed length **L** for the whole session (D15). |\n| **K** | Number of fragments in one block. Derived as `blockSize / L`; never transmitted (D7). |\n| **Block** | A contiguous slice of the (possibly compressed) payload, cut into K fragments and fountain-coded independently. **Always means this** — never \"fountain block\" or \"QR block\". |\n| **Packet** | One fountain-coded symbol: 13-byte header + L payload bytes. The unit a tile carries. |\n| **Tile** | One QR symbol on screen. Carries exactly one packet. |\n| **Frame** | One displayed image, containing a grid of tiles. **Never** a video frame — those are *camera frames*. |\n| **Camera frame** | One image captured by the receiver's camera. |\n| **Beacon** | A special **packet** carrying file-level metadata instead of payload. Beacon packets are encoded into tiles and mixed into display frames by the frame mixer (D17, §7.2). |\n| **Profile** | A modulation configuration: QR version, module pixel size, tile count. Several coexist per frame (D16). |\n| **Dwell** | How many packets the sender emits for one block before advancing (§8.1). |\n| **Screen px** | A pixel on the *sender's display*. What the renderer controls. |\n| **Camera px** | A pixel in the *receiver's captured frame*. What the decoder actually sees. |\n| **px/module** | **Always CAMERA px per module unless explicitly written \"screen px/module\".** The 4 px/module decode cliff is a *camera*-pixel figure. Conflating the two put every S2/S3 optical run below the cliff — see `../notes/spike-results.md` §S3. |\n| **Magnification** | `camera_px_per_module = screen_px_per_module × M`, where `M` = (capture width across the code region) / (code region width in screen px). A 1920-px-wide landscape code region filling a 1080-px-wide portrait capture gives **M = 0.5625**, so 4 screen px/module is only **2.25 camera px/module**. |\n| **Erasure** | A packet that did not arrive or failed validation. Never a corrupted packet — those are discarded, not used. |\n| **Stage** | A modulation generation: 1 = tiled mono QR, 2 = + RGB tripling, 3 = custom grid codec. |\n| **Pass** | One complete traversal of every block by the sender. |\n\n---\n\n## 3. What multi-gigabyte breaks, and the fix\n\nFour assumptions in the pre-multi-GB design do not survive contact with a 4 GB file.\n\n### 3.1 The fountain decoder does not scale — in TIME, not memory\n\nThis is the correction the plan review surfaced, and it matters because the first\nversion of this section got it half right.\n\nD5 chose an LT code with a **Gaussian elimination** decoder, verified at\n[`sim/`](../research/sim/). GE costs O(K²) in *memory* and O(K³) in *bit operations*.\nThe original block-layer decision sized K from the memory term alone and concluded 4 MB\nblocks (K = 16,384) were fine because the coefficient matrix is only 32 MB.\n\n**The memory term was never the binding constraint. Time is.**\n\nEach arriving packet is reduced against up to `rank` stored pivot rows; each row\noperation XORs the coefficient mask (K/8 bytes) *and* the payload (L bytes). Reaching\nfull rank costs `W = 2 · (K²/2) · (K/8 + L) = K² · (K/8 + L)` bytes of memory traffic,\nand the block only lasts `K·L / R` seconds at wire rate R — so the decoder must\n**sustain**:\n\n```\nrequired = W / (K·L/R) = K · (K/8 + L) · R / L    bytes/sec\n```\n\n> The leading factor is **1, not 2** — the 2 and the /2 in `W` cancel. A previous\n> revision of this section printed `2 · K · (K/8 + L) · R / L` and was 2× too\n> pessimistic in every derived figure. Gate **G7** now diffs this section against the\n> model so the class of error cannot recur.\n\nAll figures below are emitted by\n[`sim/ge_cost_model.py`](../research/sim/ge_cost_model.py) — this section quotes the\nmodel rather than reasoning beside it. **All rows at Stage 1 (R = 30 KB/s)**, so they\nare comparable:\n\n| K | L | Block | Matrix | Work/block | Sustained need | |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 1,000 | 1260 | 1.2 MB | 122.1 KB | 1.3 GB | 33.8 MB/s | research baseline |\n| 1,500 | 1260 | 1.8 MB | 274.7 KB | 3.0 GB | 52.9 MB/s | research partitioning ceiling |\n| 4,000 | 1260 | 4.8 MB | 1.9 MB | 26.2 GB | 171.6 MB/s | research called this **\"too slow\"** |\n| **16,384** | **256** | **4.0 MB** | **32.0 MB** | **576.0 GB** | **4.5 GB/s** | **23× over budget** |\n\nThe plan's own evidence base\n([`fountain-codes-and-protocol.md`](../research/fountain-codes-and-protocol.md) §2.6)\nstates: *\"Cost scales as K², so it must be bounded. At K = 4000 the decode work is ~16×\nthat of K = 1000 (~6 GB of XOR) — too slow\"* and recommends *\"source-block partitioning\nabove K ≈ 1500\"*. **K = 16,384 was 11× past that ceiling.**\n\nIt was worse than a simple overshoot: shrinking L to 256 B to fit small tiles made the\nmask term (K/8 = 2048 B) dominate the payload term (256 B) by 8×, so the decode problem\ngot *harder* as a side effect of a decision made for a different reason.\n\n**Two further findings from the model:**\n\n- **A faster wire rate makes decode harder** — same work, less time to do it. So K MUST\n  be sized for the *fastest* stage we intend to reach (Stage 3, 106 KB/s), not the\n  slowest. This is counterintuitive and is why the original error was easy to make.\n- **The sender's cost was unbudgeted too.** §6.3.1 counted QR encode and render but not\n  the fountain XOR. At uncapped harmonic degree and K = 16,384 that is 398 KB of XOR\n  per packet — **91.8 MB/s** at the old 225 packets/s (1 packet/tile), or **183.6 MB/s**\n  at the adopted 450 packets/s (2 packets/tile at R2 nominal), on top of everything\n  else. Hence D25.\n\n**Fix — D19:** K = **768**, L = **256 B**, block = **192.0 KB**.\n\n| | Was | Now |\n|---|---|---|\n| K | 16,384 | **768** |\n| L | 256 B | **256 B** (unchanged — see §3.1.1) |\n| Block | 4 MB | **192.0 KB** |\n| GE matrix | 32.0 MB | **72.0 KB** |\n| Block-layer working set | ~36 MB (claimed) | **264.0 KB** |\n| Sustained need @ Stage 3 | 14.9 GB/s | **114.6 MB/s** |\n\n*Both \"sustained need\" figures are at Stage 3, so they compare like with like. The\n4.5 GB/s in the table above is the same design at Stage 1.*\n\n**K_max at Stage 3 is 1152.** We adopt **768** deliberately below the ceiling —\nD26 requires the sender to assume the weaker receiver, and the 200 MB/s budget is\nitself an unmeasured estimate (§18 R1). Margin at Stage 3: **1.74×**.\n\n| K | Block | Stage 1 | Stage 2 | Stage 3 | |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 512 | 128.0 KB | 19.7 MB/s | 39.3 MB/s | 69.5 MB/s | 2.88× margin |\n| **768** | **192.0 KB** | **32.4 MB/s** | **64.9 MB/s** | **114.6 MB/s** | **adopted, 1.74× margin** |\n| 1024 | 256.0 KB | 47.2 MB/s | 94.4 MB/s | 166.7 MB/s | 1.20× margin |\n| 1152 | 288.0 KB | 55.3 MB/s | 110.6 MB/s | 195.4 MB/s | 1.02× — the ceiling |\n| 1536 | 384.0 KB | 82.6 MB/s | 165.2 MB/s | 291.8 MB/s | 1.5× **over** at Stage 3 |\n\n### 3.1.1 L is set by the *conservative* ladder rung, not the nominal one\n\nA revision of this plan briefly set L = 507 B (\"one packet per v15 tile\") and broke\nD16's ladder. D15's source note states the governing rule plainly: **pick L to fit the\nsmallest tile any profile would use.** At L = 507 the packet is 520 B and the\nconservative rung, v10-L, holds **271 B** — so it could carry **zero** packets, only\nbeacons. That destroys the ladder's one load-bearing property: *a mis-guessed profile\nyields zero; a ladder always yields something.*\n\n**Rungs are therefore defined by packet count, with the QR version chosen to fit** —\nnot the reverse. At L = 256 B, packet = 13 + 256 = **269 B**:\n\n| Rung | Packets | Needs | QR version | Capacity | Waste |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| R1 conservative | 1 | 269 B | v10-L | 271 B | 2 B |\n| R2 nominal | 2 | 538 B | v16-L | 586 B | 48 B |\n| R3 aggressive | 3 | 807 B | v20-L | 858 B | 51 B |\n| R4 (probe only) | 4 | 1076 B | v23-L | 1091 B | 15 B |\n\nWaste stays ≤ 51 B on every rung. The pressure that motivated raising L has also\ngone: at K = 768 the mask term is K/8 = 96 B against a 256 B payload (27%), not the\n8× dominance that made L = 256 pathological at K = 16,384.\n\n**A rung MUST carry a whole number of packets.** Partial packets across tiles would\ncouple tiles together and destroy the independence D1 depends on.\n\n### 3.2 Neither side can hold the file in memory\n\nA multi-GB `Uint8Array` is not allocatable (Chrome's `ArrayBuffer` ceiling is ~2 GB;\nSafari's is lower), and would get a phone tab killed regardless.\n\n**Fix — D20:** stream both ends. `File.slice()` on the sender, OPFS on the receiver, one\nblock resident at a time.\n\n### 3.3 The whole-file hash cannot be computed in one pass\n\n`crypto.subtle.digest` has **no streaming API** — it takes one buffer.\n\n**Fix:** per-block hashes (cheap, and they let each block be written as it completes,\nthen verified retroactively once the manifest arrives) plus an optional whole-file hash\nfrom an incremental WASM hasher. See §7.4 for how this interacts with `streamId`.\n\n### 3.4 Miss recovery gets expensive as blocks multiply\n\nAt 192 KB per block a 4 GB file is ~21,800 blocks. Sequential dwell means a block missed\non pass 1 waits for pass 2 — hours. **Fix:** the repair code (§8.2), which makes recovery\nsub-minute and is why smaller blocks are affordable.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Decisions\n\n| # | Decision | Rationale | Source |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| **D19** | **Block layer: independent 192.0 KB blocks, K = 768, L = 256 B** | GE cost is bound by *time*, not memory (§3.1). K = 768 keeps pace at Stage 3's 106 KB/s (114.6 MB/s needed, **1.74x margin**) within a conservative 200 MB/s phone-JS budget; matrix is 72.0 KB and the block-layer working set 264.0 KB, flat regardless of file size. K_max is 1152; 768 is deliberate conservatism per D26. **L is set by the conservative ladder rung** (S3.1.1), not the nominal one. What RFC 6330 calls source blocks. | §3.1, `sim/ge_cost_model.py` |\n| **D27** | **The receiver duty-cycles BLOCK-GRANULAR under thermal pressure; multi-GB is framed as multi-session** | Measured: a Pixel 6 hit 70 °C and its throttling threshold in **20–30 minutes**, against a §1.1 objective of 27 h–4 days of *continuous* decoding. Duty-cycling is **nearly free on this channel** — a skipped frame is an erasure the fountain code already absorbs (D5). **Block-granular approach**: the receiver knows `blockIndex` from the packet header (§7.1), so it decodes block N at full attention and skips N+1 entirely — **doubling passes rather than destroying every pass**. Frame-granular duty cycling (50% duty on every frame) is BROKEN: with 25% erasure it delivers 0.5 × 0.75 = 0.375 of packets, and dwell 1.6 yields only 0.60 K against 1.03 K needed, so blocks never complete. Drop decode *resolution* before block-granular duty cycling (superlinearly cheaper). No web API exposes SoC temperature, so sustained fps decline is the proxy (E17b). | `spike-results`, R11, bf-4h8h |\n| **D25** | **Cap fountain degree at d ≤ 64** | Cuts encoder XOR **7.9×** at the adopted K = 768 (mean degree 106.3 → 13.5): 12.2 MB/s → 1.6 MB/s at 450 packets/s (R2 nominal: 2 packets/tile, 15 tiles, 15 fps). D6 forbids changing the distribution on faith, so it was **simulated**: at the adopted **K = 768** the cap costs **+1.6 points** (1.34% → 2.97% mean, p99 4.2%), and +1.9 pts at K = 1024. There is a cliff below it — cap 32 costs +4.9 pts with a bad p99, cap 16 costs **+55 pts**. 64 is the right side of the cliff with margin. | `sim/degree_cap_sim.py` |\n| **D26** | **K is chosen by the SENDER at session start and MUST be conservative** | Decode cost lands on the receiver, whose CPU the sender cannot know (no back-channel). So the sender MUST assume the weaker device. K = 768 is the default floor; a sender-side setting MAY raise it when the user knows the receiver is a desktop, **but MUST NOT exceed K_MAX = 2048 to maintain I6a's 1 MB block-layer working set constraint**. Working set = K²/8 + K×L (matrix + block); at K = 2048 with L = 256 B this equals exactly 1 MB. The receiver derives K from the beacon and MUST refuse a stream whose K exceeds what it benchmarked locally. | §3.1, `src/core/params.ts` validateK() |\n| **D20** | **Stream both ends; never materialise the file** | Multi-GB `ArrayBuffer` is not allocatable. `File.slice()` sender-side, OPFS receiver-side. | §3.2 |\n| **D21** | **Per-packet header stays 13 bytes: file metadata lives in the beacon** | A 3-byte block index would have cost 23% more header. Moving `payloadLen`, filename, MIME, hash and block count into the periodic beacon pays for it exactly. Payload packets carry only what is needed to *place bytes*. | §7.1 |\n| **D22** | **Resume is mandatory and first-class** | At 2.7–27 h for 1–10 GB, no transfer survives on user patience. Receiver persists the completed-block bitmap; incomplete blocks restart rather than persisting partial GE state. | §1.1, §8.3 |\n| **D23** | **Estimate time before the user commits; refuse or warn at defined thresholds** | Thresholds are numeric (§13.1), not \"a threshold\". Estimate from *measured* rate once acquired. | §1.1 |\n| **D24** | **Frames generated on demand and discarded; nothing pre-rendered** | The LT stream is endless — no finite frame set exists. One pass over 4 GB is ~550,000 frames = **4.2 TB** as `ImageData`. On-demand encode costs ~7% of one core. PRNG-derived indices make the sender **stateless**: frame *N* generates without replaying 1…*N*−1, which is what makes resume and repair nearly free. | §6.3.1 |\n| D1 | **Tiled QR, not single QR** | 15 × v15 QR decode from one 1080p frame in 7.8 ms for ~7.5 KB user-visible payload (at 2 packets/tile: 15 tiles × 2 packets × 256 B = 7,680 B; 8.0 KB includes 13-byte headers). This vs 2,953 B for one v40 — ~2.5× for zero new decoder risk. | `beyond-qr` §10 |\n| D2 | **QR v15 @ ECC L, ~15 tiles** | Bounded by the 4 **camera** px/module cliff (§2 — *not* screen px), not symbology density. EC L because the channel is erasure-dominated — redundancy belongs in the fountain code. L→H would cost 57% of payload for nothing. | `qr-encoding` |\n| D3 | **zxing-wasm decoder, read `.bytes`** | Only credible multi-symbol decoder that returns real bytes — verified against 7 libraries with every byte value: exact in 100% of payloads. Bounded 9–26 ms where jsQR hit 1453 ms. Apache-2.0. | `browser-qr-scanning` |\n| D4 | **node-qrcode encoder, mask pinned** | Pinning the mask is a 4.6–8× encode speedup — a bigger lever than library choice. Worker-safe. | `qr-encoding` |\n| D5 | **LT fountain + harmonic distribution + GF(2) Gaussian elimination** | GE needs +1.2% overhead at K=1000 where peeling needs +180%. ~300 lines. **Re-measured at the adopted K = 768**: +1.34% mean / +2.5% p99 uncapped, +2.97% / +4.2% with D25's cap — inside §13.1's budget. See §18 R1 for the RaptorQ trigger. | `fountain-codes`, `sim/` |\n| D6 | **Harmonic and GE are a coupled pair — never change one alone** | Harmonic + peeling is the worst cell measured and degrades as K grows. Fails only on large inputs, pointing away from the cause. Any change to the distribution (including D25's cap) MUST be simulated first. | `sim/` |\n| D7 | **Index sets derived from a PRNG, never transmitted** | Seeded on `(streamId, blockIndex, seq)`. Zero index bytes on the wire. | `fountain-codes` |\n| D8 | **Compress before blocking, to a staging file** | `CompressionStream` is native and streaming. Compress to OPFS first, then cut into fixed blocks — keeps K constant and derivable. Skip on already-compressed input (sample-detect). Staging MUST be wiped (§12, T4a). **Trade-off: with compression enabled, resume is NOT supported** (§8.3, `notes/bf-17s0-resume-compression-conflict.md`) — `CompressionStream` offers no determinism guarantee, so re-compression after staging is reaped (E11) would produce different blocks and silently corrupt the receiver's state. | `fountain-codes` |\n| D9 | **Display at ≤ half the *measured* camera fps** | PixNet's rule. Faster produces only torn frames. | `beyond-qr` |\n| D10 | **Every frame DC-balanced** | Stops auto-exposure hunting; throughput swings 2.4× on exposure. Also part of the photosensitivity mitigation (§20.1). | `custom-codec` |\n| D11 | **A runtime calibration probe decides luma-vs-colour, not this document** | Two research threads reached opposite conclusions (§6.6). The probe measures the device. | `beyond-qr` §6.6 |\n| D12 | **Dark-on-light, not dual-polarity** | Dual-polarity costs ~50% throughput. OLED ABL means mostly-white loses ~4× brightness — \"light\" means *moderate*. | `pwa-platform` |\n| D13 | **Add to Home Screen is mandatory on iOS** | Safari deletes service-worker caches after 7 days; Home Screen apps are exempt. | `pwa-platform` |\n| D14 | **`exposureCompensation: min`; measure delivered fps, never trust `getSettings()`** | A precondition for D9. Android delivers 15 fps while reporting 30/60; the fix measured 15.0 → 41.6 fps. Absent on iOS — hence \"measured\". | `browser-qr-scanning` §1.4 |\n| D15 | **Fragment length `L` is fixed for the session — not per profile, not ever** | Change L and K changes, invalidating every packet already collected. | `link-adaptation-design` |\n| D16 | **Sender mixes 2–4 robustness profiles *within every frame*; no negotiation in v1** | Packets are fungible, so the sender never has to choose. **Probing is free** — a probe tile that succeeds delivers real payload. Mixed within a frame so profiles cannot alias against camera fps. | `link-adaptation` |\n| D17 | **Conservative beacon profile, re-emitted periodically** | WiFi's lowest basic rate. Enables late join and re-acquisition. Carries all file metadata (D21). | `link-adaptation-design` |\n| D18a | **Phase 3: the ladder runs at FIXED weights. No control loop.** | OLLA is closed-loop and its error signal (`cameraPxPerModule`) is a **receiver-side** metric, but only the sender can change rungs and D16 says no negotiation in v1. A controller with no observable cannot run. The research places fixed-weight ladders at T2/Phase 3 and weight adaptation at T4/Phase 5; an earlier revision collapsed the two. **Fixed weights (frame-area fractions): R1 (conservative v10-L) = 15%, R2 (nominal v15-L) = 60%, R3 (aggressive v20-L) = 25%. Never drop any rung below 10% in steady state.** | `link-adaptation` §10.2 |\n| D18b | **Phase 5: adapt ladder weights from LOCAL metrics only — OLLA structure, 1:9 up/down asymmetry, ~1 s window, 2 s dwell, immediate hard step-down** | Closed-loop density control oscillates; profile selection stays a **stateless lookup** so there is no state machine to get stuck in. \"Local\" means the sender's own signals (frame timing, accelerometer à la COBRA), never receiver feedback. | `link-adaptation` §10.3 |\n| D18c | **Assume 20–30% residual erasure. This is an ASSUMPTION about the channel, not a controlled target.** | Nothing in v1 observes erasure (D18a), so calling it a \"target\" was wrong. 20–30% is the evidence base's figure; driving it lower would mean the ladder is too conservative and throughput is being left unused. Dwell is sized to survive the **top** of the band (§8.1), and the repair code (§8.2) covers the tail beyond it. | `link-adaptation` §9.3 |\n\n---\n\n## 5. Invariants\n\nViolating one of these is a correctness bug, not a tuning choice. Each has an\nenforcement mechanism, because an invariant nothing checks is a comment.\n\n| # | Invariant | Enforced by |\n|---|---|---|\n| **I1** | Fragment length **L** MUST NOT change within a session (D15) | Session type makes `L` `readonly`; property test asserts a mid-session change throws |\n| **I2** | The degree distribution and the decoder MUST change together (D6); any distribution change MUST be simulated before merge | `sim/` assertions ported into the test suite; CI gate G4 |\n| **I3** | Fountain indices MUST be derived from `(streamId, blockIndex, seq)`, never transmitted (D7) | Golden test vector `(streamId, blockIndex, seq) → index set`, bit-exact across implementations |\n| **I4** | The file MUST NOT be fully materialised in memory on either side (D20) | Phase 1 flat-memory test over a synthetic 4 GB stream |\n| **I5** | **Exactly one payload block is GE-active at a time; the manifest stream has its own separate GE context** (bf-28b) | Session type permits two concurrent GE contexts: `active` for payload blocks and `manifestActive` for manifest blocks. Payload block-switch policy (`bf-2t1k`) governs when to switch: hold until rank K or N consecutive higher-index packets (default N=32). The manifest uses reserved `blockIndex = 0xFFFFFF` and `PacketFlags.Manifest`, providing clean separation from payload blocks. This is necessary because manifest blocks are interleaved with payload blocks (§7.6), and both require fountain decoding. |\n| **I6a** | **Block-layer** working set MUST stay ≤ 1 MB regardless of file size (264 KB at the adopted design) | A5 headless block-layer memory assertion |\n| **I6b** | **Whole-receiver** peak MUST stay ≤ 64 MB, and the decode pool MUST hold ≤ 4 in-flight `VideoFrame`s | Phase 3 instrumented run. A single 1080p RGBA frame is **7.9 MiB**, so this budget is dominated by the camera path, not the codec — which is why I6 had to be split |\n| **I7** | Frames MUST be generated on demand, never pre-rendered (D24) | Ring buffer is bounded at 3; assertion on buffer depth |\n| **I8** | A packet failing `fcrc` or `streamId` MUST be discarded, never applied | Unit test with corrupted and foreign packets |\n| **I9** | A block MAY be written to OPFS before its hash arrives, but MUST NOT be surfaced to the user until verified | Test: blocks written before manifest arrives are not exported; verification failure prevents completion and triggers E-BLOCK-HASH |\n| **I10** | Decoded output MUST be byte-identical to input | End-to-end property test, every phase |\n\n---\n\n## 6. Architecture\n\n### 6.1 Layering\n\n**Modulation is swappable**, and **the block layer bounds everything below it**.\n\n```\n┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐\n│ UI          role select · progress · file in/out · coach │\n├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n│ Session     metadata · compression · resume · verify     │\n├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n│ Block       file ⇄ 192 KB blocks · scheduling · bitmap   │\n├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n│ Fountain    LT encode (endless) / GF(2) GE decode        │\n│             K = 768 · matrix 72.0 KB · CONSTANT          │\n├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n│ Framing     13-byte header + payload → packet bytes      │\n├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n│ Modulation  ◄──────────────────────── SWAPPABLE ────────►│\n│   Stage 1   tiled monochrome QR                          │\n│   Stage 2   + RGB channel tripling                       │\n│   Stage 3   libcimbar-derived grid codec                 │\n├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n│ Transport   canvas render loop  /  camera capture loop   │\n└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘\n```\n\n```ts\ninterface Modulation {\n  readonly packetsPerFrame: number;     // 1 plain, ~15 tiled, ~45 tripled\n  readonly bytesPerPacket: number;      // = 13 + L\n  encodeFrame(packets: Uint8Array[]): ImageData;\n  decodeFrame(frame: VideoFrame): Uint8Array[];   // 0..n — never throws\n}\n```\n\n`decodeFrame` returning fewer packets than `packetsPerFrame` is the **normal case**.\nNothing above this layer may care.\n\n### 6.2 Threads and ownership\n\nLayer boundaries and thread boundaries are **not** the same, which is worth stating\nexplicitly because it is a common source of bugs:\n\n| Component | Thread | Owns |\n|---|---|---|\n| UI, canvas paint | main | display |\n| Frame encoder | worker | ring buffer (depth 3, I7) |\n| QR decode pool | N workers | `VideoFrame` — MUST `close()` each or the pipeline stalls |\n| GE decoder | 1 worker | the 72 KB matrix; single-owner, no sharing |\n| OPFS writer | worker | `createSyncAccessHandle` is worker-only |\n\n**Backpressure policy:** if decode falls behind capture, camera frames are **dropped, not\nqueued**. A queued frame is stale by the time it decodes, and queuing turns a throughput\nproblem into a memory problem. Dropped frames are erasures, which the fountain code\nalready absorbs.\n\n### 6.3 Sender pipeline\n\n```\nFile ──► [sample: compressible?] ──► CompressionStream ──► OPFS staging\n  │            (D8, skip if not)                              │\n  └──────────────── or straight through ─────────────────────┘\n                                                              │\n                                   cut into 192 KB blocks (D19)\n                                                              │\n                 ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n                 ▼                                            ▼\n        beacon (D17/D21) every ~2 s          per block: slice → K=768 fragments\n        filename · size · blockCount           → LT encode (d ≤ 64, D25)\n        blockSize · L · K · hash · flags       → header → tile\n                 │                                            │\n                 └──────────────► frame mixer ◄───────────────┘\n                                       │\n                          ladder of 2–4 profiles (D16)\n                                       │\n                              DC-balance (D10) ──► canvas\n                                       │\n                     display at ≤ ½ measured camera fps (D9/D14)\n```\n\nThe sender **dwells** on each block (§8.1), then advances, looping the file\ncontinuously. It never terminates on its own — it cannot know when the receiver is done.\n\n> **Beacon clarification:** The beacon is a **packet** (distinguished by `PacketFlags.Beacon` in its header), not a separate frame. The \"frame mixer\" shown above combines beacon tiles (QR-encoded beacon packets) with payload tiles into the same displayed frames. This ensures minimal overhead: the sender emits beacon packets every ~2 seconds by replacing a few payload tiles in regular frames, rather than interrupting transmission with dedicated beacon frames.\n\n#### 6.3.1 Frames are generated on demand (D24)\n\nEvery arrow above is a **generator**, not an array.\n\n- **No finite frame set exists.** The LT encoder is rateless; how many frames a transfer\n  needs depends on channel loss and is unknowable in advance.\n- **One pass would not fit.** 4 GB ≈ 550,000 frames; as 1080p `ImageData` that is\n  **4.2 TB**, ~55 GB even as PNGs.\n- **On-demand is cheap.** ~0.29 ms per v15 tile (from 1.53 ms at v40, mask pinned) ×\n  15 tiles × 15 fps ≈ **65 ms/sec, ~7% of one core**, plus ~2.3 ms/sec to render, plus\n  **fountain XOR: 3.4 KB/packet at d ≤ 64 (D25) = 0.8 MB/s** at this geometry's\n  **450 packets/s** (15 tiles × 2 packets/tile × 15 fps, using the R2 nominal rung) —\n  negligible, but only because of the cap. Uncapped it is 6.1 MB/s\n  at K = 768, and was 91.8 MB/s at the old K = 16,384.\n\nBecause indices derive from a PRNG (D7), the sender is **stateless**: frame *N* generates\ndirectly without replaying 1…*N*−1. That is what makes resume and repair nearly free.\n\n**Implementation:** worker generator → ring buffer (depth 3) → main thread paints via\n`rAF`. Deeper buffering is wasted memory (I7).\n\n#### 6.3.2 Shape the code region to the CAMERA, not the screen\n\nMeasured, and worth ~4–5× on its own. The receiver's camera has a fixed aspect and a fixed\npixel count; the sender's screen has a different one. What matters is **camera px per module**\n(§2), and that is set by how much of the capture the code region fills.\n\nA 1920×1080 landscape code region imaged by a portrait 1080×1920 capture yields **M = 0.5625** —\nso 4 screen px/module is only 2.25 camera px/module, below the cliff. Rendering the *same*\npayload into a **portrait-shaped region** inverts this:\n\n| Code region on screen | M | Camera px/module @ 2 screen px | Tiles | QR cap/frame | Payload/frame |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 1920×1080 (naive: fill the screen) | 0.56 | 1.13 — **far below cliff** | 15 | 8.8 KB | 7.5 KB |\n| 1080×1080 square | 1.00 | 2.00 — below cliff | 9 | 5.3 KB | 4.5 KB |\n| **540×960 portrait** | **2.00** | **4.00 — above cliff** | 15 | **8.8 KB** | **7.5 KB** |\n\nSame tile count and same bytes per frame as the naive layout, but *above* the cliff instead of\nbelow it — so yield goes from roughly a fifth to near-total. **The sender MUST size the code\nregion to the receiver's capture aspect, not to its own display.** Since there is no\nback-channel, it cannot know that aspect: expose it as a user-visible setting (portrait /\nlandscape receiver) **defaulting to portrait, which is how phones are held — and portrait is\na fully supported mode, not a degraded one.** The 540×960 portrait region above clears the\ncliff (4.00 camera px/module) at the *same* 7.5 KB/frame payload as the naive landscape\nlayout. **Phase 3's ≥ 20 KB/s gate MUST pass with the receiver held portrait, unaided** —\nthat is the default, unassisted case, not a stretch goal.\n\n**Packets-per-tile basis.** The R2 nominal rung (v16-L, 60% of tiles in steady state per D18a)\ncarries **2 packets per tile**. Each packet is 269 B (13-byte header + 256 B payload), so\n2 packets = 538 B per tile, which fits within v16-L's 586 B capacity. The **user-visible payload**\nis 15 tiles × 2 packets/tile × 256 B = **7,680 B/frame ≈ 7.5 KB/frame**, matching the table\nabove (per §13.2, all throughput figures quote user-visible bytes, not wire bytes). The **8.8 KB/frame\nQR capacity** is 15 tiles × 586 B (v16-L capacity). At 15 fps, this geometry delivers\n**7.5 KB × 15 fps = 112.5 KB/s payload rate** (or ~113 KB/s) before fountain overhead\nand erasure loss.\n\n**Two routes to the same M; landscape is a free bonus, not a requirement.** Physically holding\nthe receiver in landscape puts the screen's long axis on the camera's long axis — **1.78×,\nfree, and it does not require halving screen px/module the way the portrait-region layout\ndoes** — so it is worth *offering* to a user willing to turn the phone. But the app MUST NOT\ndepend on the user doing so: the sender-side portrait region (above) is the primary,\nalways-on path, and landscape is strictly an optional upgrade for extra margin on top of it.\n\nVerified negative: forcing the receiver's *OS* orientation does not help — sensor mapping\nfollows the device body, not the UI. Since portrait is the supported default, this mostly\ndoesn't matter; it only matters for the optional landscape upgrade, which needs a *physical*\nturn (§11 `E-ORIENTATION`, reframed below as a tip, not a requirement).\n\n### 6.4 Receiver pipeline\n\n```\ngetUserMedia ──► exposureCompensation:min (D14) ──► measure real fps (rVFC, ~1 s)\n      │\n      └──► requestVideoFrameCallback ──► MediaStreamTrackProcessor*\n                                                │\n                              ROI crop (conditional — see §6.4)\n                                                │\n                              ┌─────────────────┴──── Worker pool ────┐\n                              ▼                                       ▼\n                      zxing readBarcodes                     [Stage 2: split\n                      (all symbols, .bytes)                   R/G/B, stretch, ×3]\n                              │\n                    header parse ──► fcrc ──► streamId lock ──► route by blockIndex\n                              │                                        │\n                     beacon? ──┴──► learn size/blocks/K/hash    payload ──► GE decoder\n                                    (gates everything)\n                                                        rank == K ──► write to OPFS\n                                                                  ──► mark decode bitmap\n                                                                  ──► verify hash (if manifest present)\n                                                                  ──► mark verified bitmap\n                                                                              │\n                                            all blocks present & manifest decoded ──► verify all blocks\n                                                                  ──► [decompress] ──► save\n```\n\n\\* `MediaStreamTrackProcessor` is **Chromium-only**; `requestVideoFrameCallback` +\n`drawImage` is the universal fallback and MUST be implemented (§16.3).\n\n**Block-layer working set: 264.0 KB** — 72.0 KB matrix + 192.0 KB block — flat regardless\nof file size. This is *not* the whole-receiver figure; see I6a/I6b in §5.\n\nThree rules that are cheap to implement and expensive to omit:\n\n- **Measure fps, never trust it.** `getSettings()` reports 30/60 while the camera\n  delivers 15.\n- **Crop to ROI before decoding — but the 9× is conditional.** Measured 8.6× (56.9 → 6.6 ms)\n  *when the code occupies part of the frame*. Once the grid fills the frame — which is what\n  you want for camera px/module — **the ROI is the frame and the win evaporates** (69 ms).\n  ROI is a recovery mechanism for being too far away, not a throughput optimisation at the\n  right distance. **Except at high capture resolution**, where a tight quad-crop is what keeps\n  camera px/module high *and* pixel count bounded at once — there it is load-bearing, and must\n  be far tighter than the spike's 35%-margin version.\n- **Select capture resolution deliberately — it is a first-class tunable.** Measured knee:\n  720p → 100% erasure (1.5 camera px/module, nothing decodes); 1080p → best goodput; 4K →\n  zero empty frames but 194 ms decode and 1.1 fps, net *worse*. Decode is O(pixels), so more\n  resolution is not free. `getUserMedia` defaults are **not** adequate: a Pixel 6 defaults to\n  1080 on the *short* edge.\n- **Shape the code region to the camera, not the screen (sender-side, §6.3.2).**\n- **Never offer a torch button.** It measured a 3.6× fps gain, which makes it tempting,\n  but an LED on a glossy screen creates a specular hotspot that destroys a region of the\n  frame. `exposureCompensation` gets the same mechanism without glare.\n\n### 6.5 Module layout and dependency pins\n\nCommitted in Phase 0 so \"where does this go?\" is not re-litigated eight phases running.\nNote the layer boundaries of §6.1 and the thread boundaries of §6.2 are **not** the same,\nso the tree separates them explicitly.\n\n```\nsrc/\n  core/                 # pure, no DOM, no workers — the testable heart\n    fountain/           #   lt-encode.ts  ge-decode.ts  prng.ts  degree.ts\n    block/              #   partition.ts  bitmap.ts  schedule.ts\n    frame/              #   header.ts  beacon.ts  crc.ts  repair-code.ts\n    hash/               #   block-hash.ts  stream-id.ts\n  modulation/           # the swappable layer (§6.1)\n    types.ts            #   the Modulation interface — the ONLY contract above\n    qr-tiled/           #   stage 1: encode.ts  decode.ts  layout.ts  ladder.ts\n    qr-colour/          #   stage 2\n    grid/               #   stage 3\n  workers/              # one file per thread role (§6.2)\n    encode.worker.ts  decode.worker.ts  ge.worker.ts  opfs.worker.ts\n  platform/             # every capability probe and fallback lives here\n    camera.ts  storage.ts  wakelock.ts  share.ts  capabilities.ts\n  ui/                   # role select, progress, coaching, pre-flight\n  app.ts\ntest/\n  fixtures/             # conformance vectors (§14.3)\n  degradation/          # synthetic blur/glare/tear generators\ndocs/                   # plan, notes, research, sim\n```\n\n**Rules.** `core/` MUST NOT import from `modulation/`, `workers/`, `platform/` or `ui/` —\nit is the layer the property tests own. Nothing outside `modulation/` may reference QR\n(D-modulation-swappable). Every browser capability check lives in\n`platform/capabilities.ts`, never inline at a call site, so §16.1's platform matrix has\nexactly one implementation.\n\n**Dependency contract.** Exact-pinned, no ranges, no post-install scripts (gate G3).\n\n| Dependency | Pin | If unavailable |\n|---|---|---|\n| `zxing-wasm` | exact version + SRI on the `.wasm`. **MUST call `setZXingModuleOverrides({ locateFile })` pointing at a bundle-local, service-worker-precached `.wasm`.** See the warning below | Fatal on the receiver — surface `E-WASM-LOAD`; the sender still works |\n| `node-qrcode` | exact version | Fatal on the sender; the receiver still works |\n| `CompressionStream` | platform | Skip compression (D8 is already conditional) |\n| `MediaStreamTrackProcessor` | platform | Fall back to `requestVideoFrameCallback` + `drawImage` — MUST be implemented, it is not Chromium-only |\n| OPFS | platform | Refuse large files; cap at in-memory size and say so |\n| Wake Lock | platform | Warn before a long transfer (`E-WAKELOCK-LOST`) |\n\n> ### ⚠️ `zxing-wasm` fetches its WASM from a CDN by default — this voids the entire premise\n>\n> Verified in the installed package: `dist/es/core-*.js` hard-codes\n> `https://fastly.jsdelivr.net/npm/zxing-wasm@<ver>/dist/…` and fetches the `.wasm`\n> **lazily on the first decode call**, not at page load. Shipping the default means the\n> receiver:\n>\n> 1. makes a **third-party network request mid-session** — voiding T7, concept.md\n>    constraint 1, and the README's \"provably no exfiltration\";\n> 2. **fails completely in airplane mode** — i.e. in the flagship air-gapped use case (A8);\n> 3. **executes remotely-fetched WASM** — precisely the supply-chain surface T5 exists for.\n>\n> The `.wasm` MUST be bundled, precached by the service worker, and located via\n> `setZXingModuleOverrides`. §14.4's assertion covers this, and it is a **Phase 2 entry\n> criterion** because Phase 2 is the first phase that loads a decoder.\n\n**Cross-origin isolation.** The pipeline uses transferable `VideoFrame`s and\n`ArrayBuffer`s, **not** `SharedArrayBuffer` — so COOP/COEP headers are **not** required.\nThis is deliberate: requiring them would constrain static hosting for no gain. Any future\nuse of `SharedArrayBuffer` is a hosting decision, not just a code change.\n\n### 6.6 The luma-vs-colour disagreement, and how it is resolved\n\n| | `custom-codec-engineering.md` §7.2 | `beyond-qr-optical-channels.md` §6.6 |\n|---|---|---|\n| Colour cell penalty under 4:2:0 | 2× linear (4× area) — **derived** | 1.25× linear (1.56× area) — **measured** |\n| Verdict | luma-only wins ~1.95× | RGB-tripling wins **1.98×** |\n\nThe measured result is better founded and the mechanism convincing: **chroma decimation\nis a low-pass filter, not a deletion.** A binary chroma pattern at 5 px/module presents\n2.5 chroma samples per module — above Nyquist; at 4 px/module exactly 2.0, right at\nNyquist, which is where the measurement breaks.
